newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Rich nations accused of neglecting funds for nature.
newsitem.headline: Rich nations accused of neglecting funds for nature.

text.p: Rich countries came under pressure to live up to their commitments to finance conservation efforts in the developing world at the start of an international conference on biodiversity on Monday.

"There is compelling evidence that the developed countries, with the sole exception of Norway, are failing to meet their financial obligations," the Global Biodiversity Forum said in a statement released at the opening session.

The forum of specialists from public and private groups presented recommendations on a broad agenda of topics including agriculture practices, food safety, intellectual property rights and indigenous knowledge to the Third Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biodiversity.

The conference brings together delegates from 162 states that signed the Convention on Biodiversity drafted at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. The treaty aims to protect the diversity of the world's biological resources and to ensure that their benefits are equitably shared.
But critics said funds pledged in 1992 to help implement the convention in poor countries have not been forthcoming.

"If you look at whether developed countries have really come up with new money, the short answer is no," Rob Lake, senior policy officer of BirdLife International, told Reuters. "In 1992 there was a big peak in donations because everybody wanted to be seen to be green. But since then it's fallen."
And the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) said nations were dragging their feet in implementing the Convention.

"The Convention urgently needs to establish priority measures that will ensure adequate use and protection of the biological resources found in forests, marine-coastal zones and freshwater ecosystems," a WWF spokeswoman said.
"If it doesn't, it will have virtually nothing to show for its five years of existence when the United Nations General Assembly convenes next year at the Earth Summit II," she said.
Convention officials said criticism denoted exaggerated expectations for a treaty ratified only three years ago.
"This is the fastest comprehensive environmental treaty to be agreed upon, and everything's moving on schedule," said Calestous Juma, Executive Secretary of the Convention.

Lake presented the meeting with Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development data showing development aid peaked at $60.8 billion in 1992 and dropped to $56.7 billion in 1994. Other data showed the downward trend continued.

Experts said on Monday that because aid was falling, new mechanisms were needed to boost biodiversity schemes at a national level. They proposed debt swaps, tax incentives and an end to subsidies on environmentally unsound farming.

"Efforts should be redirected toward changing the incentive structure for private-sector actors, making it more profitable to conserve than to destroy biodiversity," the World Resources Institute's Charles Barber told Reuters.
